catalog_quote: [StressTyp2 passage 1540, citing Capell 1970:7] Single morpheme words are stressed on the first syllable unless the second has a long vowel. Prefixation does not alter the stress. In four syllable words, an alternative pattern with penultimate stress and initial secondary stress occurs. A suffix does not advance stress in nouns, but in verbs it may. In words consisting of more morphemes the stress is on the root. ... [Rumsey 1982:9 fn.1] For an account of Uŋarinjin stress, see Coate and Oates 1970:7-8. ... [Rumsey 1982:59] A third criterion is that loosely joined elements are stressed independently of the elements to which they are attached, one of the syllables of the postposition always bearing second degree stress (cf. Coate and Oates 1970:78), while tightly joined elements are stressed as part of the word in which they occur, hence often receiving only tertiary stress.
sweep_summary: Ngarinyin (ngar1284, weight-hedged; deciding source Capell 1970:7 known only via the StressTyp2 entry). Two title-hits: Capell 1970 'Stress and intonation' (the deciding source) and Coate 1970 'Ngarinjin stress and intonation' tape-transcription booklet. New this search of works with stress in the title: the public archive.org full-text-search API returns scanned highlight fragments from the two access-restricted scans of Coate & Oates 1970, and ~120 chained queries (both scans agree) reconstruct nearly all of pp. 7-8 (saved with raw fragments; Capell's own words: initial stress in single-morpheme words 'unless there is a long vowel in a subsequent syllable'; long vowels 'tend to attract stress'; length 'not generally phonemic' but 'linked with the stress throughout the language'; prefixation does not alter stress; noun suffixes do not advance stress but verb suffixes may; polymorphemic words stress the root; phrasal verbs stress the auxiliary. This REFINES the catalog: the 'second syllable' window in the StressTyp2 passage is a compiler narrowing (Capell: any subsequent syllable) and the 4-syllable penultimate 'alternative' is StressTyp2's reading of a CvCvCvCv schematic whose marks the scanned lost; the weight-hedged classification stands and is now anchored in the primary text (supersedes the StressTyp2 paraphrase as deciding quote). Coate 1970 booklet: transcript data only (p. 2 facsimile in held Spronck 2015 viewed: interlinear text, no stress marks, no rule), silent, low priority; booklet itself AIATSIS print-only (catalogue could not be reached by automated download). Rumsey 1982 (held) re-read: defers to Coate & Oates 1970:7-8, confirms. Still unread/paywalled: Jepson & Ennever 2023 (medium), Goedemans 2010 (low). Remaining gap for the page images themselves: the stress diacritics on Capell's CvCvCvCv/CvCvCv displays (medium priority). all lookups were direct downloads.

While vowel length is not generally phonemic in Ngarinjin, there are certain cases where stress plus length of vowel must be regarded as so [...] In words of this type a syllable containing a long vowel tends to attract stress. new_statements.reading: Default initial stress in monomorphemic words, overridden by a long vowel in ANY later syllable (Capell says 'a subsequent syllable', not 'the second'); length is admitted to be only marginally phonemic and 'linked with the stress throughout the language', so the weight condition is real but hedged — exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding. Polymorphemic words stress the root; noun suffixes never, verb suffixes sometimes, advance stress; prefixes never do. The StressTyp2 clauses 'unless the second has a long vowel' and 'in four syllable words an alternative pattern with penultimate stress and initial secondary stress' are the compilers' verbalisations: the first narrows Capell's window, the second renders his CvCvCvCv/CvCvCv pattern display whose diacritics the scanned did not preserve. new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the first syllable of a monomorphemic word; a long vowel in any later syllable attracts the stress instead (weight condition hedged, since Capell says vowel length is 'not generally phonemic' and is 'linked with the stress throughout the language'). Polymorphemic words stress the root morpheme; prefixes never move stress, noun suffixes do not, verb suffixes and certain enclitics (-di, indirect-object markers on the -ma- auxiliary, emphatic -dju) can advance it. Syllable count sets an alternating pattern: even-syllable words CvCvCvCv, odd-syllable words CvCvCv (Capell's diacritics on these schematics are lost in the scanned).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Present. Word-level: the CvCvCvCv / CvCvCv schematics imply alternating secondary stresses (diacritics not recoverable from the scanned fragments). Phrase-level: in phrasal verbs 'the main stress is that of the auxiliary; the invariable root assumes only a secondary stress, marked here by a grave accent' (2.3, p. 8); demonstratives lose stress and become enclitic to the preceding noun; 'At the most a secondary stress develops'; a non-monosyllabic pronominal suffix (-naŋga) also takes a secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: (1) A long vowel in a non-initial syllable attracts stress (ŋanda:renjiriwalu vs ŋandarenjiriwalu; stress+length marginally contrastive). (2) Verb suffixes may advance stress: 'a:ŋga 'he went' > a'ŋga:lu 'he came'. (3) Enclitic -di and emphatic -dju move stress forward (be'lendju 'afterwards'); indirect-object markers on the -ma- auxiliary are enclitic (njinma're:ra 'you did it to me'), tense markers are not. (4) The -ma- auxiliary keeps initial stress ('ŋi:ma, 'njinma) while the wu ~ o 'strike' auxiliary carries main stress on its root (a'ŋoni, an'dja:wi). (5) 'Prefixes, however, are not causes of moving an accent back.' (6) Noun suffixes never advance stress (win'djaŋun > win'djaŋun-da).
new_statements.identity_note: Coate & Oates 1970 describe Ngarinjin (= Ungarinyin/Ngarinyin, ngar1284) of the Kimberley, Western Australia; the stress section is Capell's, based on Coate's material. No dialect is named in the fragments I could see. The Spronck 2015 facsimile held by the project (Coate 1970, 'Ngarinjin stress and intonation', Tape Transcription Series 1, p. 2) is a transcribed dialogue page with no stress statement; it is the companion tape booklet Capell's section refers to, not the listed work.

new_statements.relation_note: Same primary source as the catalog's existing statements (Capell's section 2 in Coate & Oates 1970) and the same placement: default initial stress in monomorphemic words, overridden by a long vowel — this is the print origin of the 'unless the second has a long vowel' clause that the existing statement already identifies as the StressTyp compilers' narrowing of Capell's 'a subsequent syllable'. It adds the StressTyp code [I/I] (bounded initial/second quantity-sensitive type), three examples, and the chapter's remark that Ngarinyin shows traces of right-oriented stress. It does not contradict the catalog's weight-hedged coding; note the code [I/I] confines the weight window to the second syl…
new_statements.rule_in_words: StressTyp's rendering of Capell 1970: in monomorphemic words primary stress is initial unless the second syllable has a long vowel, in which case that long syllable is stressed. The code [I/I] is defined in the appendix (p. 847) as 'Place stress on the initial syllable if it is heavy (even if the second syllable is also heavy), otherwise place stress on the second syllable if it is heavy, if neither first nor second syllables are heavy, then place stress on the first syllable' — i.e. a bounded left-edge quantity-sensitive system with long vowels as the heavy syllables. The examples show initial stress on a word with a long initial vowel (ˈdaːwuru) and on a plain word (ˈŋudmanda), and stress on the long root vowel of a prefixed verb (wa-ŋan-ˈdaːrenjiriwalu). Goedemans's own chapter (p. 81) adds only that, from Coate & Oates 1970, Ngarinyin shows 'traces of right oriented stress', which he flags as needing more research.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing: the StressTyp entry lists no secondary-stress clause and marks no secondary stresses in its three examples; the chapter says nothing about Ngarinyin secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The rule is stated for single-morpheme words only; the third example shows that in a prefixed verb the stress sits on the root's long vowel rather than on the word-initial prefix. The chapter's 'traces of right oriented stress' (p. 81) is the only hint at non-initial patterns and is not spelled out for Ngarinyin. The entry's bibliographic line misattributes the grammar to 'Oates, H.H.J. & L. Oates' (should be Coate & Oates).
new_statements.identity_note: The StressTyp entry heads 'Ngarinyin; Ungarinjin', classified 'Australian, Wororan, Ungarinjinic. Derby to King River, Kimberley, Western Australia' — the same language as ngar1284; no dialect is distinguished. Its sole source is Capell's 'Stress and intonation' section in Coate & Oates 1970 (miscited there as 'Oates, H.H.J. & L. Oates (eds.)'). The chapter's citation line in READALL_TARGETS mentions 'Miriwung = language no. 51 on the stress map'; that note belongs to a different item — Ngarinyin is not on the Figure 1 map at all (checked the cue list, p. 66).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between sources on placement: the StressTyp entry (p. 682) and Capell 1970 (the catalog's existing statements) both give initial stress in monomorphemic words unless a long vowel attracts it. The only tension is one of scope and hedging: StressTyp/Goedemans narrows the long-vowel window to the second syllable (code [I/I]) whereas Capell wrote 'a subsequent syllable', and StressTyp omits Capell's caveat that vowel length is only marginally phonemic and 'linked with the stress'. Goedemans's chapter sentence that Ngarinyin shows 'traces of right oriented stress' (p. 81) is an interpretive gloss on Coate & Oates 1970, not a placement statement, and is compatible with Capell's root/suffix-advanced stress in polymorphemic words; it does not amount to a penultimate claim for the language.
